messages.content: Write an internal post about making security everyone's responsibility at a software company. Around 250 words.

**Security isn't the security team's job**

AppSec is four people. Roughly 210 of us ship code. A review request sits in their queue six days on average, and that number has nothing to do with how hard they work.

We can't hire our way out. Eight people gets us a three-day queue, and a three-day queue still trains everyone the same way: file the ticket last, cross your fingers, ship regardless.

Here's what's different starting now.

Threat modeling belongs in the design doc. No separate template, no approval step. One section: what would an attacker try here, and what stops them. Fifteen minutes at a whiteboard, typed up by whoever owns the doc. AppSec reads those sections. They stop writing them.

Every service gets an owner on the hook for its dependencies, its secret rotation, and how it handles auth. "The platform team" is not an owner. A human name in the service catalog is.

We're also publishing the five worst things that have actually happened here since 2024. Real incidents, redacted only where we have to. Generic training slides evaporate. "Remember the open S3 bucket in March" sticks.

And when you spot something, in your code, a teammate's, or a vendor's, raise it fast and in public. Nobody here has ever been punished for finding a hole. The one unacceptable move is seeing it and saying nothing.

That gives four people room to do what four people can do: think hard about the genuinely hard designs, and build guardrails the rest of us get by default. A checkpoint people learn to route around helps nobody.

Ask in #security. Start with whatever design doc you open next.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
**Security isn't AppSec's problem to carry alone**

Four people work in AppSec. About 210 of us write code that ships. Their review queue runs six days deep, and that has nothing to do with effort.

Hiring won't fix the math. Double the team and the queue drops to three days — but a three-day queue teaches the same lesson a six-day one does: file the ticket at the end, hope, ship anyway.

So we're changing where the work lives.

Threat modeling moves into the design doc. No separate template, no sign-off gate. Add a section: what would someone attack here, and what stops them. Fifteen minutes at a whiteboard, written up by whoever owns the doc. AppSec reads those sections instead of authoring them.

Every service gets a named owner responsible for its dependencies, its secret rotation, and its auth handling. "The platform team" doesn't count. A person's name in the service catalog does.

We're also publishing the five worst things that have actually gone wrong here since 2024 — real incidents, redacted only where legal requires it. Generic training slides fade in a week. "Remember the open S3 bucket in March" doesn't.

When you find something, in your code or anyone else's or a vendor's, say so quickly and out loud. No one at this company has ever been penalized for finding a hole. The only wrong move is noticing and staying quiet.

Then four people can do what four people are actually good at: thinking hard about the genuinely hard designs, and building guardrails the rest of us inherit for free. A checkpoint people learn to dodge protects nothing.

Questions in #security. Start with the next design doc you open.
